name: Just-world hypothesis
statement: People need to believe the world gives everyone what they deserve, and defend that belief by finding fault in victims whose suffering they cannot undo.
meaning: Two claims travel under one name and they need separating. The first is descriptive. People differ in how strongly they endorse statements like 'people get what they deserve', and that endorsement can be measured and correlated with other things. The second is causal. Watching an innocent person suffer, with no way to help, is said to push observers into judging that person more harshly. Melvin Lerner's theory joins the two. He argued the belief is a working assumption people need in order to invest in the future, so evidence against it has to be neutralised, and rewriting the victim's character is one cheap way to neutralise it. The evidence for the two claims is not the same evidence, and the verdict below is about the second.

origin.who: Melvin J. Lerner and Carolyn H. Simmons
origin.where: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
origin.note: Their paper is "Observer's reaction to the 'innocent victim': Compassion or rejection?". Its reference list cites Lerner's own 1965 paper in the same journal, on evaluation of performance as a function of the performer's reward and attractiveness, as the source of the theory it tests. He set the theory out at length in a 1980 book.

evidence: Lerner and Simmons recruited 75 female students, run in groups of four to ten. Three were dropped for having learned the setup in advance, leaving 72 spread across six conditions of 9 to 14 observers. Each watched a ten-minute videotape of a peer, in fact a confederate, appearing to take painful electric shocks for errors on a paired-associate learning task. Observers then rated her on 15 evaluative bipolar scales, with each rater's own self-rating subtracted, so lower scores mean a harsher judgement. What changed the ratings was what observers were told came next. Those who voted to move her into a rewarded second session, and were told the vote had carried, gave -5.07. Those told the experiment was over gave -12.85, and those shown her afterwards, unharmed and paid, gave -11.10. Those who voted but were not told the outcome gave -25.18. Those told they would watch her suffer again gave -25.78. Harshest were observers in the martyr condition, who had seen her reluctantly agree to be shocked so that they could earn their course credit, at -34.00. The overall test was F(5, 66) = 4.00, p < .005. A second measure, five questions on the victim's social stimulus value, gave F(5, 66) = 3.86, p < .005; a similarity measure gave F(5, 66) = 1.08 and no reliable differences.

replication.headline: Pooling 55 experiments run between 1966 and 2016, derogation of an innocent victim came to d = 0.15, and how vividly the suffering was shown predicted how large it was.
replication.detail: Dawtry, Callan, Harvey and Gheorghiu assembled 55 experiments with 5,947 participants, 40% of them unpublished and 47% reporting a nonsignificant result. The pooled effect was d = 0.15, SE 0.06, 95% CI [0.03, 0.27], p = .013. Heterogeneity was large, Q(54) = 225.64, p < .001. Their own coding places the 1966 experiment at g = 0.89, SE 0.33, near the top of the set. The moderator was how the suffering reached the observer, scored by having 60 people rank nine ways of learning about another person's misfortune, from a computerised ball-tossing exclusion game up to watching someone suffer in person. That score predicted the size of derogation, b = 0.13, SE 0.04, 95% CI [0.05, 0.21], p < .001. It was confounded with year of appearance, because older studies were both more impactful and larger. Small-study bias showed up in the overall model, Egger's test z = 2.28, p = .022, and was undetectable once emotional impact was included. Trim-and-fill imputed seven missing effects on the low side, and weight-function models placed the overall estimate between -0.205 and 0.153 while leaving the moderator between 0.102 and 0.160. The authors conclude that publication bias makes the derogation effect probably smaller than their estimate. Their own Study 2 gave 561 people one of four real CCTV robberies or a text description of the same events. Ratings of the victim relative to the rater were more negative after video, d = 0.29, 95% CI [0.12, 0.45], p < .001, while absolute ratings did not differ, d = 0.04, 95% CI [-0.21, 0.29], p = .61. Study 3 repeated this on 801 people and made half the victims a drug dealer. Video moved ratings of the innocent victim and not of the guilty one, F(1, 797) = 10.96, p < .001, and, against the authors' expectation, the relative and absolute measures behaved alike this time.

study.cite: Dawtry, R. J., Callan, M. J., Harvey, A. J., & Gheorghiu, A. I. (2020). Victims, vignettes, and videos: Meta-analytic and experimental evidence that emotional impact enhances the derogation of innocent victims. Personality and Social Psychology Review, 24(3), 233-259.

limits: The verdict is about the causal claim, that seeing an innocent victim suffer makes observers judge the victim more harshly. The measurement claim stands separately and stands better. Rubin and Peplau's Just World Scale, Lipkus's Global Belief in a Just World Scale and Dalbert's Personal Belief in a Just World Scale all yield scores that vary between people. Their internal consistency varies too. Hellman, Muilenburg-Trevino and Worley's reliability generalisation gives mean alphas of .81 for the Lipkus scale, .68 for the 1975 Rubin and Peplau revision and .64 for the 1973 version, figures read off the published abstract rather than the paywalled article. Preregistered repeats of the 1966 procedure exist and have not been published. Dawtry and Callan filed three on the Open Science Framework in September and October 2016. Two follow Lerner and Simmons and one follows Lerner's 1971 study, each comparing the midpoint condition against a milder one on the same 15 bipolar scales. The second registration records that the first attempt was stopped after seven participants because too many saw through the deception. The project holding them is private, so no result from any of the three could be obtained. The early wave of repeats sits in the meta-analysis and not only in its prose. Dawtry's table codes Lerner's three 1971 studies at g = 0.87, 1.69 and 0.88, Kenrick and colleagues at 1.13, and Lincoln and Levinger at 0.57. Simons and Piliavin come out at 0.53, Sorrentino and Hardy at 0.55, and Stokols and Schopler at 0.46. Searches of Crossref, PubMed, Europe PMC, OpenAlex and the OSF registry found no published meta-analysis pooling just-world scale scores against victim blaming. One is registered on OSF, filed on 6 July 2025 by Huang and colleagues, whose form states the analysis is finished and the manuscript being written. Russell and Hand's rapid evidence assessment is the nearest published work and pools nothing. Nine articles survived their screen and four were reviewed in detail. They report just-world belief positively associated with rape myth acceptance, and call the literature on just-world belief and victim blame inconclusive. Qiu and Tang's three-level meta-analysis of 51 studies and 247 effect sizes concerns student well-being rather than blame, and its pooled correlations could not be obtained. Twardawski and four colleagues published experiments on just-world beliefs and victim blaming in the Journal of Experimental Social Psychology in 2025. The publisher refused automated requests for the text and no other copy was found, so nothing from it appears here. The pooled figure above comes from heterogeneous laboratory paradigms rather than from repeats of the 1966 design. Hafer and Bègue's review of post-1980 experiments discusses the unsystematic nature of that research, which is one reason a single pooled number is hard to interpret.
misreadings: The idea is usually stated as a claim that people blame victims because they believe the world is fair. Lerner and Simmons measured character ratings of a stranger, not attributions of blame, and the two need not move together. The theory is also said to predict less derogation whenever observers can act. Acting was not enough in the study itself. Observers who voted to have the victim rewarded but were not told whether the vote had carried gave -25.18, as harsh as those expecting to watch her suffer again, and only those told it had carried gave the mildest ratings. The experiment is further cited as evidence that people are indifferent to suffering. What it shows is narrower: the harshest ratings came from observers who thought she had agreed to suffer for their benefit. A small pooled effect is not a licence to say derogation never happens. It says the average across mixed laboratory materials sits near zero, while vivid depictions of suffering still move ratings. Three neighbouring entries carry material that gets run together with this one. Defensive attribution hypothesis, no. 251, is blame rising with the severity of an accident. System justification, no. 168, is the defence of an arrangement rather than of one victim's character. Fundamental attribution error, no. 11, is reading behaviour off the person, which needs no justice motive at all.
